Concepts#

Five ideas explain everything else in these docs: scenes are compiled, compiled scenes stream, the viewer picks a tier, every scene is signed, and a scene is addressed by one id that works everywhere. This page is the mental model; the how-to guides are the hands.

Compile, don't convert#

A builder's model or a photogrammetry scan is far too heavy to send to a browser whole. Verse does not shrink it — it compiles it once, server-side, into a container built for streaming (.vpk for meshes, .vsp for Gaussian-splat captures):

  • The mesh is cut into thousands of small clusters, each simplified into a hierarchy of detail levels (coarse at the top, source detail at the bottom) with seams locked so neighbours never crack.
  • Textures are encoded for the GPU (BC7 / ASTC-class via UASTC) and sorted by importance: the materials covering the most world surface get full streamed textures — up to 4096² for a "hero" tier, and base colour above 4096 (8K, 16K) as virtual-texture pages streamed at the resolution each pixel needs — and the long tail lives on a shared 1024² preview atlas.
  • A walk-collision grid, a spawn point, an automatic ~30 s tour and a 2D floor plan are derived and written beside the file.
  • The whole thing is laid out so that the first bytes are the most useful ones: a few MB of header and coarse levels open the scene; the rest is fetched by byte range only when a camera wants it.

Compile cost is roughly 8 seconds per source MB on the production box (estimateS on the job record): a minute or two for a product, about twenty minutes for a 3-million-triangle building. Draco, KHR quantization and KTX2 inputs are normalized on the way in. Uploaded sources are deleted after compile; the compiled scene is what is kept and served. (The one exception is a model published in compatibility mode, where the uploaded GLB is the scene.)

Streaming is a cut through a hierarchy#

The viewer never downloads a scene. Every frame, a GPU pass decides which clusters — at which detail level — would project to roughly one pixel of error on this screen from this camera, and the residency loop fetches exactly those by HTTP Range request, evicting what the camera left behind. Consequences you will notice:

  • Scene size stops mattering. A 30-million-triangle scan and a chair cost the viewer about the same per frame; the metrics wall holds both above 100 fps on the same laptop.
  • Latency matters more than bandwidth. Refinement is a chain of small range requests, so a far-away viewer is RTT-bound. That is why an edge cache near the viewer (see the cache headers in the API reference) roughly halves time-to-sharp, and why private scenes — which never touch a CDN — are slower for remote reviewers by design.
  • First seconds are tuned deliberately. Coarse clusters carry a baked flat colour, so the opening frames read as a soft clay model with correct colours while textures arrive, instead of shattered glass. The ?vgflat knob exposes it.
  • Streaming is observable. progress events report drawn/total clusters; the ?inspector=1 panel shows residency per level; the stats channel carries everything else.

Gaussian splats stream the same way at the chunk level (.vsp: full and coarse subsets per chunk, chosen by projected size).

Tiers: what each device gets#

The viewer classifies the device once at boot and the whole stack adapts:

TierBackendWhereWhat changes
AWebGPU, desktop-class GPUlaptops, desktops, high-end tabletseverything: SSR, reflection probes, HDR output, 4K hero textures, full post chain
BWebGPU, mobile-class GPUphones, mid tabletssmaller texture pools, lean post chain (no DoF/bloom), no SSR, no hero pool
CWebGL2in-app browsers, older devicesa separate bundle, held to its own golden images on every release, that renders classic scenes and opens streamed scenes with a CPU-selected cut (compared against tier A per scene by fix-verify-tierc-stream); studio lighting, contact shadow, bloom, optional SSAO, per-room reflection probes and real-time GI; no SSR, ray-traced reflections, TSR or path-traced stills; splats need WebGPU

Dynamic resolution scaling keeps frame time inside the display's budget on every tier, and on-demand rendering parks the loop when nothing changes (the default in embeds and on battery). The embed SDK reports the tier in its ready event and a degraded event when it had to step down; the final rung is a poster image with a link out, so an embed never shows a blank box. The matrix of browsers and WebViews is in Browser support.

Fidelity: two paths#

Verse is measured against ground truth, not eyeballed. (This section is about how faithfully streamed scenes reproduce their source. **Fidelity mode** — a textured product or scan published as itself, at source resolution, with no streaming — is a different thing: Fidelity mode.)

  • Baked scenes (archviz exports whose lighting is already in emissive lightmaps) must reproduce the bake bit-faithfully: unlit materials bypass tone mapping, post effects that would alter a bake are suppressed, and lightmaps are never encoded with a banding codec. The harness renders the source bake in Blender EEVEE and gates the streamed result at a 64×64 mean ΔE76 below 6 per view (web/test/fidelity.mjs); our apartment scenes measure 0.6–2.5.
  • Lit scenes (plain PBR with live lights) are compared with EEVEE given the same scene, sun and environment through the engine's own display transform; gate ΔE below 9 (web/test/fidelity-lit.mjs). At the last audit ten of eleven reference views measured 0.5–8.2; one view of a scratched-metal helmet sits at 12 and is open work.

Screen-space reflections, HDR output and the vertex-tangent path are each gated separately so they can never drift the fidelity numbers; the quality knobs let you turn each one on or off per link.

Signed, and verified where it is viewed#

Every compiled file is signed Ed25519 by the server that compiled it (a descriptor in the header and a trailer after the directory for .vpk; an 80-byte trailer for .vsp). The browser fetches the origin's public key (GET /v1/pubkey) and verifies with WebCrypto from the bytes it already holds, then reports signed: true | false | "unverified" on the status line and in the SDK's signed event. The trust anchor is the page embedding the scene, not the host serving the bytes — so a CDN, a mirror or a copied file can never make a tampered scene verify, and a missing signature never blocks loading. (The container's byte layout is an in-repo document for the team; it is not published here.)

One id, four surfaces#

A finished compile returns a scene id — the ingest/<id>.vpk part of its share link — and that id is the handle everywhere:

SurfaceHow the id is used
Share linkhttps://HOST/?vpk=ingest/<id>.vpk — opens the playground viewer; &share=<token> for a private scene; &tour=, &experience= compose more
Embed<script src="https://HOST/embed.js" data-scene="<id>"> or Verse.embed(el, { scene: "<id>" })
API/v1/scenes/<id>/… (ownership, visibility, share tokens, stats), /v1/review/<id> (pinned comments), GET /v1/ingest/<id> while the job record lives
Studiothe scene card at /studio — poster, link, embed snippet, analytics, visibility and share links

Ownership is the one thing layered on top: scenes uploaded anonymously are retained best-effort under a disk budget; scenes uploaded with (or claimed by) an account are permanent, can be made private, and roll up analytics. Accounts are token-only — the token is the credential, like an API key.

Where the pieces run#

Code
your page / Blender / Unity / Unreal / curl
        │  HTTPS (plain JSON + raw bytes)
        ▼
 one Node service ── ingest API, signing, share links, review, rooms, telemetry, docs
        │  spawns             │  serves by byte range
   verse-compile          ingest/<id>.vpk  ──►  (optional CDN edge)
   (native Rust)                                      │
                                                      ▼
                                browser: main thread (UI only)
                                  ├─ sim worker  (camera, walk, collision)   ─┐ shared-memory
                                  └─ render worker (Rust→wasm, WebGPU/WebGL2) ─┘ triple buffer

The browser's main thread never renders (design law #1): the engine lives in a render worker, the simulation in another, and they exchange frames through a lock-free triple buffer in shared memory. That is why the page stays responsive under the heaviest scene, and why the server must send the cross-origin-isolation headers the engine iframe carries for you.
